flashcards.q: What are the three phases of a Lambda cold start, in order?
flashcards.a: Download/pull the package or image, then INIT (runtime bootstrap plus any global-scope code, runs once per execution environment), then INVOKE (the handler runs per call). After INVOKE the environment freezes and can be thawed later, skipping INIT.

flashcards.q: Typical cold start p50 for Java without SnapStart vs with SnapStart?
flashcards.a: 5-15+ seconds without SnapStart (JVM boot and class loading dominate) versus 90-140ms with SnapStart, because SnapStart restores a snapshot taken after init already ran once instead of rebooting the JVM from zero.

flashcards.q: Which runtimes have GA SnapStart support as of the 2024-2025 rollout?
flashcards.a: Java 11+, Python 3.12+, and .NET 8+ (which also covers C#, F#, and PowerShell). Regional availability expanded significantly through 2025 -- verify current region coverage before an interview since this keeps changing.

flashcards.q: What is the SnapStart gotcha around randomness and credentials?
flashcards.a: Anything generated during init (random seeds, cached credentials, unique IDs) gets frozen into the snapshot and would be identical across every cold start restored from it, unless you explicitly re-randomize or refresh them in a beforeCheckpoint/afterRestore runtime hook.

flashcards.q: Is Lambda-in-a-VPC still a major cold-start penalty in 2026?
flashcards.a: No. The 2019 Hyperplane networking change replaced per-execution-environment ENI creation (which took 10-15 seconds) with pre-created ENIs shared per subnet+security-group combination. VPC attachment today adds well under 50ms. The remaining VPC cost is a NAT Gateway bill for internet egress, not latency.

flashcards.q: Difference between reserved concurrency and provisioned concurrency?
flashcards.a: Reserved concurrency sets a floor-and-ceiling on how much of the account's concurrency pool one function can consume, guaranteeing isolation but not eliminating cold starts. Provisioned concurrency pre-initializes a fixed number of warm environments, eliminating cold starts for invocations within that count, at a continuous hourly cost.

flashcards.q: What happens when you exceed available Lambda concurrency for a synchronous invoke?
flashcards.a: The caller receives a 429 TooManyRequestsException (throttling) -- Lambda does not queue synchronous invocations, so the caller must implement its own retry/backoff.

flashcards.q: What are the default event source mapping batch sizes for SQS vs DynamoDB Streams/Kinesis?
flashcards.a: 10 for SQS; 100 for DynamoDB Streams, Kinesis, and MQ/MSK.

flashcards.q: What does ReportBatchItemFailures fix, and what does it NOT fix?
flashcards.a: Without it, one failed message in a batch causes the entire batch to be retried, including already-succeeded messages. Enabling it lets the handler return only the specific failed item IDs so just those retry. It does NOT eliminate the need for idempotency -- the source is still at-least-once delivery regardless.

flashcards.q: How do sync and async Lambda invocation retry semantics differ?
flashcards.a: Synchronous invokes (API Gateway, direct Invoke) are never retried by Lambda -- the caller must retry. Asynchronous invokes (S3, SNS, EventBridge) are queued internally and retried automatically by Lambda, by default about 2 additional attempts, invisible to the original caller.

flashcards.q: How does memory relate to CPU allocation in Lambda, and what are the key thresholds?
flashcards.a: CPU is allocated proportionally to configured memory, not set directly. At 1,769 MB a function gets the equivalent of one full vCPU; at the 10,240 MB maximum it gets roughly 6 vCPUs. Memory is configurable 128MB-10,240MB in 1MB increments.

flashcards.q: Why can raising Lambda memory sometimes lower total cost, and when does it not help?
flashcards.a: Billing is duration x memory, so if more memory (more CPU) cuts duration by more than proportionally, total cost drops. It doesn't help I/O-bound functions waiting on a downstream call, since CPU isn't the bottleneck there -- use AWS Lambda Power Tuning to find the actual optimum rather than guessing.

flashcards.q: What is Lambda's maximum execution timeout, and why is it fixed rather than extendable?
flashcards.a: 900 seconds (15 minutes), a hard limit by design that bounds how long any tenant can occupy shared execution capacity. It cannot be worked around safely by chaining self-invocations; use Step Functions, Fargate, or AWS Batch for longer work instead.

flashcards.q: Name four situations where Lambda is architecturally the wrong choice even though it would technically work.
flashcards.a: Steady high/predictable throughput (loses the cost crossover to always-on compute), jobs needing more than 15 minutes, GPU-dependent inference workloads (zero GPU support), and infrequently-invoked functions with large slow-initializing dependencies where cold starts dominate latency.

flashcards.q: What fraction of production Lambda invocations experience a cold start, per AWS's own published data?
flashcards.a: Under 1%, concentrated in low-traffic functions and the first invocations after a new deploy.
